title: Enterprise roles UX notes (RBAC v2) — Console role assignment, warnings, onboarding copy
body:
Context
- This doc captures PM + Design notes for the Console UX for RBAC v2 roles/permissions. It is intentionally a working document.
- Primary goals: (1) make default roles easy to understand + assign, (2) reduce accidental over-privileging, (3) make security reviewers confident (separation of duties + auditability), (4) set expectations for phased support of custom roles.

Attendees / input sources
- PM: Naomi Feldman (RBAC), Marissa Cole (Console PM)
- Design: Tessa Morgan (Admin UX lead)
- Eng: Felix Schneider (audit views), Chloe Martin (console backend lead—async), Kaitlyn Nguyen (authz implementation)
- Security/GRC: Marcus Lin (product security), Olga Petrov (GRC)
- Corp identity advisory: David Kim (SSO/group mapping)
- SE/CS feedback (notes): Markus Klein, Rachel Kim (from enterprise evals)

What we’re designing (first milestones)
1) Role assignment UI (Org + Project scope)
2) Role visibility in user + service accounts list
3) Permission-denied UI patterns (403 w/ reason codes, how we message + what we reveal)
4) “High-risk permission” warning patterns during assignment + review
5) Admin onboarding copy (first-login, “set up secure access” checklist)

Assumptions / constraints
- RBAC v2 primitives: resources/actions/scopes; default roles exist; policy evaluation is centralized (ref: RBAC v2 overview + authz-check standard).
- We will ship with default roles first. Custom roles likely phased behind enterprise support / later GA.
- Must support Hosted/Dedicated/Private customers. Private has additional constraints for policy distribution and needs clarity in UI (policy version, last updated).
- Auditability matters: we should log role changes + show in audit log UI.

Default roles (working set + UX positioning)
Proposed default roles to surface in Console (names can be adjusted, but copy should not change semantics):
- Org Admin
  - Full admin; can manage org settings, projects, members, SSO config, and most security settings.
- Security Admin
  - Manages SSO/SAML, SCIM, audit log export/config, security settings; does NOT manage billing by default.
  - NOTE: CISO feedback (Marcus relaying Aisha request): default should be stricter for audit-log export permissions (no “Billing Admin can export logs” by default). Keep export/config under Security Admin (and Org Admin).
- Billing Admin
  - Billing contacts, invoices, payment methods; should not be able to change access controls or security settings.
- Developer
  - Typical day-to-day: create/manage API keys within project scope, view usage, view models, manage non-sensitive project settings.
- Read-only
  - View-only; no key creation; intended for auditors and observers.
- Support (Impersonation) / Break-glass
  - Not customer-assignable in self-serve UI (ideally). When enabled, should be behind explicit approvals, time-bounded, and surfaced with strong warnings.

Design principle: separation of duties should be visible
- We should explicitly call out “Billing is separate from Security” in UI copy so customers understand why a billing admin can’t export audit logs.
- Avoid implying that Org Admin is required for day-to-day. Encourage least-privilege via onboarding checklist.

Scopes: Org vs Project
Decision (tentative):
- Role assignment happens at two levels:
  - Org-level roles: Org Admin, Security Admin, Billing Admin, Read-only (org)
  - Project-level roles: Developer, Read-only (project)
- UX should make scope explicit in the UI and in copy (e.g., “Security Admin (Org)” vs “Developer (Project: X)”).

Information architecture (IA) proposal
Left nav additions/changes:
- Organization Settings
  - Members
  - Roles & Access (new)
  - SSO & Provisioning
  - Audit Logs
  - Billing
- Project Settings (per project)
  - Members
  - API Keys
  - Usage
  - Integrations

Entry points for role management
- Primary: Org Settings → Roles & Access
- Secondary: Org Settings → Members → select member → “Access” tab
- Project: Project Settings → Members (project-scoped assignments)

Key screens & interactions

1) Roles & Access (Org) — Overview
Goal: give admins a clear picture of “who has what” with minimal clicks.
UI elements:
- Summary cards: Org Admins / Security Admins / Billing Admins / Members w/ no org role
- Table: member list with columns:
  - Member (name/email)
  - Org roles (chips)
  - Project access (count + link)
  - Last role change (timestamp + actor, if available)
  - Status (active/invited/provisioned)
- Primary actions:
  - Invite members
  - Assign org role(s)
  - Review high-risk access (filtered view)

Open question: multi-role assignment
- Do we allow multiple org roles on one principal?
  - Practical: yes (e.g., early-stage customers). But we should warn when someone holds both Billing Admin + Security Admin if we decide that’s undesirable.
  - Proposal: allow multi-role, but show “Separation of duties” hint and provide recommended split.

2) Assign role modal (Org)
Modal flow:
- Step 1: Select member(s) (search, includes invited/provisioned)
- Step 2: Select role
  - Role list with short descriptions + “Includes” highlights (not full permission list in MVP)
  - “Learn more” links to doc/tooltip
- Step 3: Confirm
  - Confirmation summary including high-risk warnings, and “This change will be recorded in audit logs.”

High-risk warnings in modal
We need a consistent rubric. We already have P0/P1/P2 sensitivity in permission inventory methodology. UX mapping:
- P0 = “High risk” (red)
- P1 = “Sensitive” (amber)
- P2 = “Standard” (no warning)

Modal warning patterns (draft copy)
- If role includes any P0 permissions:
  - Title: “High-risk access”
  - Body: “This role can perform high-impact security or operational actions (e.g., manage SSO, export audit logs, rotate org secrets). Assign only to trusted admins. All actions are audit logged.”
  - Require checkbox: “I understand and approve granting high-risk access.”
- If assigning Security Admin:
  - Add note: “Recommended to have at least two Security Admins to avoid lockout.” (but careful—some customers want a single owner)
- If assigning Org Admin:
  - Add note: “Org Admin can grant themselves any role and manage all settings.”

We should avoid listing exact sensitive endpoints (security-through-obscurity vs transparency). Recommendation: show examples at a high level (SSO settings, audit log exports, role changes), not internal endpoint names.

3) Member detail → Access tab
Goal: single place to answer “what can this person do?”
Sections:
- Org roles (chips, editable if you have permission)
- Projects (table): project name, project role(s), last updated
- Effective access summary (read-only text): “This member can manage billing, view audit logs, and create API keys in Project X.”
  - Note: Effective summary should be generated from role, not raw permission list (MVP).

Non-goal (MVP): full permission diff view. Might be needed later for custom roles.

4) Project member management
Project-level “Assign role” should default to Developer. Read-only should be easy.
Guardrails:
- If a user has no org role but has project Developer access, that is expected.
- If a user has project access but org role is Read-only (org), clarify that org read-only does not override project developer (avoid confusion).

Custom roles vs default roles (phased plan + UX implications)

Phase 0 (MVP / GA1): Default roles only
- UI surfaces default roles with clear descriptions.
- “Custom roles” is not in-product, but provide:
  - A link: “Need a custom role? Contact support” (or “Talk to your account team”) shown only for eligible tiers (Dedicated/Private/enterprise plan).
  - A “Common requests” accordion: “Export audit logs without billing”, “Manage API keys but not deployments”, etc.

Phase 1: Limited custom roles (Enterprise)
- Provide a “Create role” workflow for org admins/security admins.
- Permission selection UI must be careful (see below). Likely separate workstream.

Phase 2: Full policy management (Private, advanced)
- Expose policy bundle version info, role templates, and possibly import/export.
- Must coordinate with Private policy distribution mechanism and signing.

Custom role builder — early notes (NOT for MVP)
- Permission list is too granular for most customers; they will misuse it. Consider grouping permissions into “capabilities” with embedded P0/P1 warnings.
- Proposed structure:
  - Capability categories: Identity & Access, Audit Logs, Billing, Projects, API Keys, Deployments, Dedicated Capacity, Private Admin.
  - Each capability has a risk label (High/Sensitive/Standard) and short explanation.
- Must include an “Effective access” preview and change log.

Permission denied UI patterns
We need two modes:
- End-user: actionable, not scary, minimal internal detail.
- Admin: enough signal to debug (role missing, scope mismatch) without exposing policy internals.

Proposed patterns
- When an action is denied:
  - Toast/banner: “You don’t have permission to do that.”
  - CTA: “Request access” (opens modal to message org admin/security admin; for SSO-provisioned orgs, may say “Contact your administrator”).
  - Secondary link: “View required role” (shows “Org Admin or Security Admin required” where safe).

Do we show reason codes?
- Backend will have 403 reason codes (per standard). UI can map a subset to friendly messages:
  - SCOPE_MISMATCH → “You have access in a different project.”
  - ROLE_REQUIRED → “This action requires Security Admin.”
  - FEATURE_FLAG_DISABLED → “This feature isn’t enabled for your org.” (only if applicable)
- Avoid showing raw permission strings in MVP (e.g., “auditlog.export”). This is helpful for power users but can create support load.

Admin onboarding copy (first-login + “secure setup” checklist)
Entry points:
- After org creation (or first enterprise admin login), show a dismissible “Secure your organization” card.
- Also show in Roles & Access page until completed.

Checklist items (draft)
1) Add a second Org Admin (avoid lockout)
2) Assign Billing Admin (so finance can manage invoices without full admin)
3) Assign Security Admin (separation of duties)
4) Configure SSO (if enterprise)
5) Enable audit log export (if available)

Copy draft (card)
Title: “Set up roles for least-privilege access”
Body: “Redwood supports separation of duties. Start with default roles (Org Admin, Security Admin, Billing Admin, Developer) to reduce risk and simplify audits.”
Buttons: “Review roles” (primary), “Learn about roles” (secondary)

Copy draft (tooltips)
- Org Admin tooltip: “Full access to org settings, members, roles, security, and billing.”
- Security Admin tooltip: “Manages SSO and audit logs. Recommended for security owners. Does not manage billing by default.”
- Billing Admin tooltip: “Manages invoices and payment methods. Cannot change roles or security settings.”
- Developer tooltip: “Build and operate projects: API keys, usage, model access within assigned projects.”
- Read-only tooltip: “View access for audit and review. No changes, no key creation.”

SSO group mapping UX (enterprise)
Problem: Many enterprise customers will want “map Okta groups → roles.”
- In MVP, this may be configured in SSO settings; role assignment UI should:
  - Indicate when a role is “Managed by SSO” vs manually assigned.
  - Prevent manual edits if SCIM/SSO is authoritative (or allow but warn about drift).

Proposed UI affordances
- Role chips with icon + label: “Managed by SSO”
- On edit attempt: “This member’s access is managed by your identity provider. To change it, update group membership.”

Audit log visibility (UX coordination)
Requirements:
- Every role assignment/removal should emit an audit event (and ideally include actor, target, role, scope, policy version).
- Console should provide an audit log filter for “Access changes.”
- Felix to align with audit log event taxonomy + surfacing.

Open questions / decisions needed
1) Who can assign roles?
- Likely: Org Admin can assign any org role; Security Admin can assign Security Admin + Read-only? (needs final policy decision)
- Billing Admin should not assign roles.

2) “Support impersonation” exposure
- Strong preference: do not expose “Support” role in customer UI.
- If we must, it should be hidden behind a feature flag and show heavyweight warnings + time bounds.

3) Dedicated/Private operational roles
- Dedicated autoscaling/GPU pool config is sensitive; does that live under Org Admin only, or create an “Ops Admin” later?
- For MVP, keep it under Org Admin (and possibly Security Admin) to avoid role explosion.

4) Custom roles messaging
- What exact copy do we use so customers don’t feel blocked?
  - Suggestion: “Custom roles are available for enterprise plans. Contact your account team.”
  - Provide a lightweight intake form (desired capabilities, constraints) rather than exposing raw permissions.

5) Display of policy version (Private)
- Private customers asked in security reviews: “Which policy bundle version is installed?”
- Proposal: show under Roles & Access page footer: “Policy bundle vX.Y (updated DATE)” with link to docs.

Action items
- Tessa: wireframes for Roles & Access overview + assign modal + high-risk warning state (target: by next design review)
- Naomi: confirm default role descriptions w/ Marcus + Olga; incorporate CISO ask re: audit log export restrictions
- Felix: audit event names + UI filter proposal for access changes
- Kaitlyn: confirm which reason codes are stable and safe to map in UI
- David: recommend best practice language for SSO-managed roles (avoid implying Redwood is source of truth)

Notes from enterprise feedback (SE/CS synthesis)
- Customers want:
  - separation-of-duties story in one screenshot (roles page)
  - ability to give auditors read-only and export logs without billing access
  - clarity on “who changed access, when” (audit events)
- Pain today (RBAC v1): “Everything is basically admin.” We need to highlight that default roles are opinionated and safe.

Appendix: UI copy alternatives (rough)
High-risk warning (short):
- “This role grants high-risk security access. Assign only to trusted admins.”
High-risk warning (explicit):
- “This role can change identity settings and export audit logs. Misuse could impact security and compliance.”
Denial message (user):
- “You don’t have access to this setting. Ask an Org Admin or Security Admin for access.”
Denial message (admin):
- “Access denied due to missing org role (Security Admin required).”

(End of notes — expect churn as policy + role semantics finalize.)
